problem: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MetaGPT, CAMEL, AutoGen) coordinate through human-assigned roles. Existing heterogeneous multi-robot systems (HMRS) rely on hand-crafted task decomposition and allocation protocols. Neither lets agents reason about what each robot can physically do (mobility, sensing, arm reach) from its hardware, and no benchmark tests this 'embodiment-aware reasoning' across diverse robot types.
motivation: In an HMRS, what a robot can do is set by its physical composition, not by a role label. Examples: wheeled robots cannot climb stairs, Spot's jaw camera cannot see high shelves, and Stretch reaches farther horizontally than Fetch. The authors argue that embodiment-aware reasoning is the missing piece for 'level-4' fully automated HMRS (automated decomposition, coalition formation, allocation and execution), which LLM agents might provide.
key_idea: Have each robot's LLM agent build its own 'robot resume' from its URDF: an LLM summary of the URDF skeleton plus numeric capabilities computed with forward-kinematics tools. A leader-plus-robot-agents discussion then uses these resumes to plan and assign subtasks feasibly, before each agent executes its subtask by function calling.
insight: Textual self-description from the URDF skeleton is enough for coarse capabilities (wheels vs legs, drone = high view), but numeric, tool-computed capabilities are needed for precise manipulation. Removing the numerical part barely matters for navigation/perception but drops single-floor rearrangement SR from 28.35% to 9.20% and multi-floor rearrangement from 13.46% to 3.85%. Replacing self-generated resumes with human role descriptions (CAMEL/MetaGPT-style) cuts overall SR from 37.82% to 15.63%, close to having no group discussion at all (15.23%). The no-discussion variant even beats the role-play variant on navigation (22.42% vs 14.14%), suggesting role play can increase hallucination. Side studies show JSON resumes work best (0.7 vs 0.3 for natural language on 10 perception episodes), and SR degrades as the team grows (80% with 2 Fetch robots, 50% with 10) because of hallucination in long contexts.
method: Scene context (provided by the benchmark, not EMOS itself): a Hydra-style 4-layer map built from ground truth. The layers are (L1) a region connectivity graph, (L2) a semantic mesh, (L3) agent/object states and (L4) a Recast navmesh. L1 and L3 are turned into text by iterating over regions and listing their objects and robots; L2 and L4 serve low-level planning.

Robot resume: a per-robot JSON covering mobility, perception and manipulation. Each capability has an LLM-written summary from a pruned URDF tree skeleton (links as nodes, joints as edges; inertial/visual/collision tags removed) plus numeric details from forward-kinematics tool calls, e.g. arm workspace as a hull of sampled end-effector positions and camera pose/FOV frustum.

Centralized group discussion (HMAS-2 star topology): a leader LLM (CentralPlanner) decomposes the task and assigns subtasks. Each robot-dedicated agent then checks feasibility against its resume (Reflection), using common-sense reasoning plus generated Python in an interpreter for spatial checks such as arm reach vs. object height/distance or target angle vs. half-FOV. Its feedback triggers reassignment.

Decentralized parallel action execution: each robot agent asynchronously picks the next action by LLM function calling over skill APIs (navigate_to, move_arm_to, pick, place), conditioned on its subtask and its action/response history. It enters a wait state when done, and the episode ends when all agents are waiting.

Low-level skills: navmesh greedy path following (Habitat navigation) and an inverse-kinematics solver using ground-truth object positions. Physics (PyBullet) is disabled and grasping is snap/contact-based.

Habitat-MAS benchmark: built on Habitat with 27 multi-floor MP3D scenes and 34 HSSD scenes, and robots Fetch, Stretch, Drone (DJI M100 model) and Spot. It has 4 tasks: cross-floor object navigation (MultiON extension), cooperative perception for manipulation, single-floor rearrangement, and multi-robot/multi-object/multi-floor rearrangement. Episodes are filtered so each robot can finish only a subset of subgoals (XOR of oracle positive/negative role assignments; geodesic/Euclidean ratio > 1). Metrics are SR, PDDL sub-goal SR, token usage and simulation steps.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (May 2024 API, frozen) for leader and robot agents
setting.observation: no raw sensor input to the LLM: textual scene description (region connectivity graph + object/agent states) from ground-truth semantic mesh and odometry, plus self-generated robot resumes from URDF
setting.action_space: high-level skill function calls (navigate_to, move_arm_to, pick, place, detect) executed by a classic navmesh planner + IK with snap grasping
setting.privileged: ideal SLAM: GT semantic mesh / region graph / object and agent states given as text; GT object world coordinates for skills; navmesh; physics disabled with snap grasp

numbers.eval_set_note: 519-episode subset of the full Habitat-MAS dataset (all 4 tasks); used for all experiments due to budget constraints
numbers.extra: perfect perception (GT scene graph as text), oracle low-level skills with physics disabled and snap grasp; own benchmark with no external baselines

numbers_note: Per-task success rates (Tasks 1-4) are shown only in Figure 6. The text quotes a few of them: navigation '37.37% → 14.14%' and perception '52.94% → 28.32%' are ambiguous as to whether the first value is EMOS or the w/o-Numerical ablation, so they are omitted. Ablation rows (w/o Numerical 23.56% SR, w/o Robot resume 15.63%, w/o Discussion 15.23%) are not entered as own variants. Side experiments on 10-episode samples are not entered: resume format (NL 0.3, JSON 0.7, Markdown 0.5, XML 0.6), robot-number scaling (2/4/6/10 Fetch robots: 80/60/70/50% SR) and object-number scaling (1/2/3/5 objects: 90/80/80/70%). The paper says 'more than 70 distinct scenes' but lists 27 MP3D + 34 HSSD scenes.
results: On a 519-episode subset of Habitat-MAS with GPT-4o, EMOS reaches 37.82% SR and 81.26% sub-goal SR, using 80,783 tokens and 2,358 simulation steps. It beats all ablations: w/o numerical resume 23.56%, w/o robot resume (human role descriptions, CAMEL/MetaGPT-like) 15.63%, and w/o group discussion 15.23%. The no-discussion variant uses the fewest tokens (36,377). The hardest task is multi-floor rearrangement, where EMOS gets only 13.46% SR, and EMOS has the best tokens-per-success efficiency (2135.99).
limitations: Relies on privileged, idealized inputs: a perfect SLAM/scene graph given as text, ground-truth object coordinates for skills, physics disabled with snap grasping. It is simulation only, with no real robots.
Evaluated only against its own ablations on its own benchmark (a 519-episode subset), with no external multi-agent or planning baselines. Absolute success is low (37.82% overall, 13.46% on Task 4).
LLM hallucination in numeric/spatial code (e.g., wrong reach computation) and poor scaling with more agents (SR falls to 50% with 10 robots) limit robustness.
builds_on: HMAS-2 (Chen et al. 2024, scalable multi-robot LLM collaboration)
compares_to: EMOS w/o robot resume (human role description, CAMEL/MetaGPT-style)
